On the one hand, the text is extremely compressed, assumes a great deal of prior knowledge, and is sometimes almost impenetrable. It constantly alludes to contemporary history, academic politics, and details of Schmitt’s own life.

Schmitt also liked to use a single line of poetry to summon up an entire mood. Because he was speaking to himself, he did not need to explain further. But an outside reader cannot always understand the meaning so easily.
For this reason, Glossarium clearly requires commentary.
On the other hand, the complexity and richness of the text can very quickly make commentary endless.

The editors have therefore chosen to keep their commentary short and restrained. They do not laboriously repeat information that is now easily available to anyone on the internet. In particular, they make no attempt to engage with the now almost unmanageable body of secondary literature on Schmitt.
Carl Schmitt cared about making his books accessible through more than just a table of contents. He was not above preparing detailed subject indexes himself.
He also began work on a subject index for Glossarium. These preliminary notes appear on the endpapers of the notebooks and are reproduced in the appendix.
The indexing is incomplete and unsystematic, but it shows that Schmitt understood the importance of his text and wanted to make its contents easier to navigate.
That is not a simple task, given the complexity of Glossarium and its frequently aphoristic or heavily abbreviated character.
After some consideration, the editors decided not to provide a subject index.
There is, of course, an index of names.
As a concentrated expression of Schmitt’s thought, Glossarium is written in constant relation—sometimes explicit, sometimes unspoken—to both his published and unpublished work.
The commentary appendix provides references intended to encourage deeper reading, although these references are by no means exhaustive.
Glossarium cannot replace serious engagement with Carl Schmitt’s wider work. But it can serve as a doorway into that work.

The book was written during a period that threw Schmitt off the established path of a middle-class scholar’s life. He viewed the new situation with resentment, but also with something like Tocqueville’s sharp-sightedness of the defeated.

Henning Ritter described this new situation in a birthday article for Wolfgang Schivelbusch published in the FAZ on 21 November 2011. Writing about Schivelbusch’s book The Culture of Defeat, Ritter said:

The book also helps explain why, after the Second World War, the victors no longer left it to the defeated to create their own myths about the postwar period. Instead, the victors themselves organized the culture of defeat. Culture became another battlefield on which victory and defeat were once again at stake. It mattered too much in the process of coming to terms with defeat to be left entirely to the defeated.
This edition could not have been produced without the help of a number of deeply committed people.
This is especially true of Dietrich Nithack, who transcribed the previously unpublished texts directly from the original manuscripts.

Until his death, Hans Gebhardt transcribed those parts of Schmitt’s text written in Gabelsberger shorthand, insofar as this was possible with notes that were usually added later and written down very hastily.
As they have done before, Florian Meinel, Wolfgang Schuller, and Wolfgang H. Spindler provided the editors with valuable clarification and assistance.
The same is true of Harald Bluhm, Peter Heyl, Wolfram Hogrebe, Ernst Hüsmert, Günter Maschke, Matthias Meusch, Andreas Raithel, Angela Reinthal, and Christian Tilitzki.
Corrections to the first edition that Günter Maschke and Piet Tommissen (†) had kindly collected some time ago have been incorporated into the new edition.

Last but not least, thanks are due to the State Archive of North Rhine-Westphalia in Duisburg for making the materials available; to Florian Simon and Heike Frank for overseeing the publishing and printing of the new edition; and to Jürgen Becker, administrator of the Schmitt estate, for permission to use and reproduce all materials important to the edition.

At night: noble simplicity and quiet grandeur. Yes—quiet!
The quiet of ordinary people living quietly in the land. Pietist and humanist quiet.
But quiet in opposition to what?
“Quiet” becomes a polemical idea aimed against the noise of the Baroque. That is the most concrete thing about this quiet and noble simplicity.
Rousseau as archaeologist: cheerful feelings awaken as Greece is dug out of the earth.
What, then, was this supposed trahison des clercs—this “betrayal of the intellectuals”? There certainly was a betrayal.
The intellectuals themselves were shamefully betrayed, worse even than King Peter of Yugoslavia. They were betrayed to money and to the masses.

And when they looked to the state for protection—which was an understandable mistake, and one that showed they still had some historical memory—when they turned to the only refuge that seemed to remain, this was then held against them as proof of their own “betrayal.”
Repulsive frauds. Destroyers of every refuge.
But God transforms the lie even in the liar’s own mouth and gives it the meaning of truth.
Trahison des clercs can also mean betrayal of the intellectuals. Grammatically, “of the intellectuals” can make them the object of the betrayal rather than its perpetrators.
And that gets to the heart of the matter: spiritual authority is destroyed by intellectuals who have gone crawling for shelter under the ruler of this world.

Speech by Enrico Corradini, Florence, 8 February 1925: presenting fascism as “the revolution of the State against the predominance of private interests.” So this is Sallust fleeing from money into the arms of Caesar.
The virgin takes refuge with the pimp.
The state Corradini fled to wanted to become a Caesarian empire.
Classicism came with it free of charge.
State = sovereignty = decision = the ending of civil war within the state. And it is only through this ending of civil war that the state itself comes into being.
Does world rule likewise mean the end of civil war? No. It means combining war between states with civil war.
Tacitus, Histories I.2: “foreign war and civil wars intertwined.”
Otto Brunner (Land und Herrschaft, 1939, p. 170): on the soil of the medieval West, sovereign powers did not exist and could not exist.

During the great struggle over investiture, the Church allied itself with local powers and thereby created “a situation in which kings and princes, caught between the Church and local powers, were unable to attain a sovereign position.”
Between spirit and soil, there can be no sovereignty! Or, more strongly: alongside a potestas spiritualis—a spiritual power—there can be no sovereignty.
A desperate unity. A unity born of desperation. That is what this sovereignty based purely on decision amounts to.
Unity only in an emergency and only in the exceptional case.

Brunner says, referring to K. H. Ganahl’s Studien zur Geschichte des kirchlichen Verfassungsrechts im 10. und 11. Jahrhundert (1935, p. 7), “that the problem of sovereignty between state and Church cannot, in any event, be raised before the Investiture Contest.”
Neither emperor, prince, nor pope was truly sovereign.
“But as long as sovereign powers did not exist” within the medieval West, “a separation between the idea of law and positive law could not establish itself” (p. 170).
So: disappearance of spiritual power → sovereignty → positive <…> legality.

In the afternoon: deeply affected by Willy Haas’s May 1932 essay “A New Political Doctrine” in Die Literarische Welt. He calls me a nihilist. He says that defining politics through the distinction between friend and enemy is itself a concealed—and indeed the worst—form of neutralization.
Why? Because it abstracts from what he sees as the one concrete cause of hostility that actually matters now: material hostility, meaning class hostility toward the bourgeoisie.
By abstracting from this, he says, my definition neutralizes that conflict and is therefore itself intensely political.
At the same time, he falsely assumes that I understand the enemy as something that can simply “be removed from this world in a war of annihilation.”
